conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim is 'substantially supported, not false' when referring to prescription-grade oral cannabidiol as an add-on therapy, citing randomized controlled trial evidence and FDA approval.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
## Conclusion

The claim is **substantially supported**, not false—when “cannabidiol” means the tested, prescription-grade oral formulation used **as add-on therapy** in children/adolescents with treatment-resistant Dravet syndrome. It should not be generalized to over-the-counter CBD products, all seizure types, or long-term outcomes.

**Best evidence:** two short, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials.

* In the original 14-week trial, 120 patients aged 2–18 received cannabidiol 20 mg/kg/day or placebo in addition to existing treatment. The trial’s primary outcome was convulsive-seizure frequency. A secondary “50% responder” result was 43% with cannabidiol versus 27% with placebo, but that comparison itself was not conventionally statistically significant (P=0.08). This is a potential source of skepticism, but it does not overturn the positive primary seizure-frequency result.  
  https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28813226/  
  https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5716495/

* A later 14-week dose-ranging RCT randomized 199 children to 10 mg/kg/day, 20 mg/kg/day, or placebo. Reported convulsive-seizure reductions were 48.7% and 45.7% with the two cannabidiol doses, versus 26.9% with placebo. The authors concluded both doses produced clinically relevant reductions; 10 mg/kg/day had better safety/tolerability.  
  https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7052786/

Regulatory decisions are consistent with this evidence: FDA labeling indicates prescription cannabidiol for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome (age ≥1 year). This is not proof by itself, but supports that the evidence met an efficacy/safety threshold.  
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2021/210365Orig1s011lbl.pdf
